sweep_summary: Only one stress-titled item exists for sanj1285: Kalstrom & Pike 1968 (Phonetica 18:16-30), already in our bibliography and already the catalog's secondary source. It is about word stress in this language. We hold only pp. 19-26 (Rosetta Project scan; copied to with). this search of works with stress in the title re-read those pages against the page scan: they describe two stress types realised as consonant length (type-one) or vowel length (type-two), and p. 26 shows root stress being dropped in favour of stress-bearing suffixes (-n·a 'my', -n·ci 'little', -ʔ·ya neg.), which confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding drawn from the 1995 Gramatica sec. 0.3-0.3.3. The missing section 1 'Stress' (pp. 16-18, the formal placement statement) and pp. 27-30 could not be obtained: Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all report the DOI (10.1159/000258596) closed with no repository copy; the De Gruyter Brill landing page returned an empty 202 and Karger a 403; HathiTrust holds Phonetica v.18-19 search-only; SIL archive entry 3726 (live) is a record only; archive.org has no other Popoloca phonology item; Google Books returned nothing; web.archive. Priority medium for the complete article (same analysts as the 1995 grammar; unlikely to change the classification). No new source supersedes the catalog's deciding source.

new_statements.quote: A morpheme which has the sequence /iy/ or /ow/ loses the consonants /y/ or /w/ when the preceding /i/ or /o/ is no longer lengthened due to stress type-two. That is, a morpheme may have both one syllable and two syllable allomorphs: ni·³yo³ tortilla, nio³n·ci¹ a little tortilla; ko²ni·⁴ya⁴ dog, ko²nia⁴n·a¹³ my dog; so·¹²wa² hot, soa¹ʔ·ya² not hot; no·³wa³ corn, noa⁴n·a²³ my corn.

new_statements.locator: p. 26 (p. 8 of the 8-page Rosetta excerpt), section (5) 'Syllable', 5th paragraph; checked against the page scan
new_statements.reading: Stress in Atzingo Popoloca is realised as length (type-one: a lengthened syllable-initial consonant; type-two: a lengthened vowel), and a root's stress is removed when a stress-bearing suffix such as -n·a 'my', -n·ci 'little' or the negative -ʔ·ya is attached, the suffix taking the stress. This is the same accent shift to tonic suffixes that the 1995 Gramatica (sec. 0.3.3) states, so it confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding. It is not new: the excerpt was already held and cited as the catalog's secondary source; the article's own placement statement (sec. 1, pp. 16-18) remains unread and no open copy of it exists.

tone_statements.quote: Popoloc, Chocho, and Ixcatec have three contrastive level tones, which are present in both the lexicon and the grammar: High (H), Mid (M), and Low (L) (for Popoloc see Veerman-Leichsenring 1991, for Chocho see Veerman-Leichsenring 2000a, for Ixcatec see Fernández de Miranda 1959). [...] Similar to Proto-Popolocan, Mazatec has a fourth level tone (K. Pike 1948: 96), as does the Popolocan variety of San Juan Atzingo. Moreover, Mazatec has phonologically contrastive contours, which are best described as sequential (K. Pike 1948: 12, 97, Beal 2011: 223). The Popolocan languages also have high tone downstep, tone sandhi, and grammatical tones.

tone_statements.quote: Como todas las lenguas en la familia otomangue, las lenguas popolocanas son tonales. Tienen melodías basadas en tres niveles de tono (alto, medio y bajo) o en cuatro (alto, medio-alto, medio y bajo), los cuales se combinan de diversas maneras. Las ortografías de las diferentes lenguas representan el tono así como los sonidos de distintas mane- ras. Los tonos pueden pertenecer a las palabras mismas, por ejemplo, ijní [īhn ̋] ‘ocho’, ijni [īhnī] ‘plato’, ijnī [íhnì] ‘sangre’ (popoloca de San Juan Atzingo); a varios procesos de flexión, por ejemplo, [ʃènʔuà] ‘fumo’, [ʃènʔuā] ‘fumas’ (popoloca de Mezontla)
tone_statements.translation: Like all languages of the Otomanguean family, the Popolocan languages are tonal. They have melodies based on three tone levels (high, mid and low) or on four (high, mid-high, mid and low), which combine in various ways. The orthographies of the different languages represent tone, as well as the segments, in different ways. Tones may belong to the words themselves, e.g. ijní 'eight', ijni 'plate', ijnī 'blood' (San Juan Atzingo Popoloca); to various inflectional processes, e.g. [ʃènʔuà] 'I smoke', [ʃènʔuā] 'you smoke' (Mezontla Popoloca)

sources.note: Sec. 2.4 states the Popolocan languages have complex tone systems; Popoloc, Chocho and Ixcatec have three contrastive level tones (H, M, L) present in lexicon and grammar, while San Juan Atzingo Popoloca, like Mazatec and Proto-Popolocan, has a fourth level tone; the family also has high-tone downstep, tone sandhi and grammatical tones. Sec. 2.5 adds that lengthening of stressed syllables is described for Atzingo Popoloc (Kalstrom & Pike 1968). Second-hand for Atzingo (rests on K&P 1968), consistent with the four tones in the held K&P excerpt.

sources.note: Sec. 4 says all Popolocan languages are tonal, with melodies built on three tone levels (alto, medio, bajo) or four (alto, medio-alto, medio, bajo) that combine in various ways; lexical tone is exemplified with San Juan Atzingo Popoloca ijní 'ocho' / ijni 'plato' / ijnī 'sangre'; tone also marks inflection (Mezontla example) and discourse (Ayautla Mazatec); it adds that men in San Juan Atzingo whistle the language. Sec. 5 lists 'alternancia de la melodía tonal de la raíz' as a person-marking device in the genus. It does not state which languages have 3 vs 4 levels.
